lessons.title: Offices, High-Street Shops, Mall Units and Warehouses

children.text: Drive along the Gurugram expressway and you will pass two kinds of commercial buildings. Some are gleaming single-owner tech parks, fully leased to global companies. Others are malls and office towers sold unit by unit to hundreds of small investors in the late 2000s, many still half-empty today. Both are "commercial real estate". The difference between them is the most important lesson for any individual who wants to own a shop, an office or a warehouse: in commercial property, what you buy matters, but who controls the rest of the building matters just as much.

body.text: A commercial unit is only as good as the building it sits in. Offices, shops, malls and warehouses each have their own economics, but all of them live or die on location, building quality and who is in charge of filling it.

children.text: Offices: Grade A Campuses and Strata Units

markDefs.definition: Office units sold individually to different buyers within one building, so ownership of the building is fragmented across many owners.

children.text: Offices are the largest commercial segment and the one most individual investors think of first. They split into two very different worlds. Grade A offices sit in large tech parks and business districts, often with a single institutional owner, professional management and tenants such as GCCs, banks and consulting firms. Individuals mostly own this world indirectly through REITs. The other world is
strata offices
: smaller units in buildings with many owners, typically let to SMEs, startups, CA and law firms, and clinics.

body.title: Grade A campus vs strata office building

columns.label: Grade A, single owner
points: Large floor plates suited to big corporates
Owner controls tenant mix and upgrades
Tenants: GCCs, MNCs, large Indian firms

columns.label: Strata building, many owners
points: Smaller units, often 500 to 3,000 sq ft
No one controls tenant quality or upgrades
Access for individuals: buy a unit directly

markDefs.definition: The area on which office rent is charged, including a share of common spaces such as lobbies, lift areas and washrooms. Similar to super built-up area in residential property.
Carpet area divided by chargeable area. An efficiency of 70% means that for every 100 sq ft a tenant pays for, 70 sq ft is usable.

children.text: Office rent is usually quoted per sq ft of
chargeable area
, not the space the tenant actually uses. The ratio between the two is called
efficiency
, and tenants care about it a great deal because it sets their real cost per usable sq ft.

body.latex: \text{Rent per Carpet sq ft} = \frac{\text{Quoted Rent per Chargeable sq ft}}{\text{Efficiency}}
body.caption: Office efficiency in India commonly falls somewhere around 65% to 75%.

children.text: A Pune office quoted at ₹90 per sq ft of chargeable area with 70% efficiency costs the tenant ₹90 ÷ 0.70 = about ₹128.6 per usable sq ft. A competing building at ₹95 with 78% efficiency costs ₹95 ÷ 0.78 = about ₹121.8. The "cheaper" quote is actually the more expensive space, and an informed tenant will choose the other building. Poor efficiency makes your unit harder to lease.
High-Street Shops: Paying for Footfall

A high-street shop is the commercial asset Indian families have owned for generations: a ground-floor unit on a busy road with a pharmacy, a jeweller or a mobile phone store as tenant. The economics depend almost entirely on footfall, visibility and frontage. A corner unit on Brigade Road in Bengaluru or Linking Road in Mumbai commands far higher rent than an identical-sized shop one lane back, and a ground-floor unit earns many times what the first floor above it does.

body.text: For shops, width beats depth. A 15-foot frontage with a 30-foot depth is usually worth more to a retailer than an 8-foot frontage with a 60-foot depth of the same area, because shoppers decide from the pavement.

children.text: Tenants range from national brands, which sign longer leases and pay reliably, to local businesses that come and go. High-street shops are easier to understand and often easier to sell than other commercial units, but they are exposed to changes you cannot control: a new metro line that shifts foot traffic, a flyover that blocks visibility, or a mall opening nearby.
Mall Units: The Strata Trap

A mall is not a collection of shops. It is a managed business that needs the right mix of anchor stores, brands, food courts and entertainment to draw visitors. Successful Indian malls, such as those run by Phoenix Mills, DLF or Nexus Select Trust, keep ownership with one entity that curates tenants, runs marketing and reinvests in the property.

Many malls built in the 2000s were instead sold unit by unit to individual investors. With hundreds of owners, nobody controlled the tenant mix, and each owner leased to whoever paid. The mall lost its draw, footfall fell, brands left, and a spiral of vacancy followed. Consultants have repeatedly flagged such underperforming "ghost malls" across Indian cities.

body.text: Be very cautious about buying an individual unit in a strata-sold mall. Your rent depends on footfall that you have no ability to influence, and in a failing mall an empty unit may find neither a tenant nor a buyer at almost any price.

markDefs.definition: A mall lease structure where the tenant pays the higher of a fixed minimum rent or a percentage of its sales from that store.

children.text: Mall leases also work differently from other commercial leases. Many use a
minimum guarantee plus revenue share
structure, which ties the owner's income to how well the store performs.

body.label: Why owners like revenue share
body.context: The minimum guarantee protects the owner in weak months, while the revenue share lets rent rise automatically when the mall is busy. This only works when the owner can see the tenant's sales, which is why it suits professionally run malls.

children.text: Warehouses: Big Boxes, Long Leases

markDefs.definition: A property constructed to one tenant's specific requirements, usually in exchange for a long lease commitment from that tenant.

children.text: Warehousing has become India's fastest-growing commercial segment, driven by e-commerce, third-party logistics and manufacturing. Grade A warehouses in institutional parks, built by developers such as IndoSpace, Welspun One and Horizon Industrial Parks, have high ceilings, proper truck docks, fire safety systems and long leases. They are often
built-to-suit
for a single tenant.

Rent per sq ft is a fraction of office rent, often in the region of ₹20 to ₹35 a month, but warehouses are large and cheap to build. Most of the value is in the land, the location close to highways and consumption centres, and the approvals. Hubs like Bhiwandi near Mumbai also hold large amounts of older, unorganised Grade B stock, where unclear approvals and fire safety gaps are common risks.

body.title: Newer formats: data centres, cold storage and life sciences

children.text: Data centres, cold chains for food and pharma, and lab space for life sciences companies are growing fast in India. They need specialised power, cooling and construction, and are almost entirely developed and owned by large institutions. Individual investors usually get exposure through listed companies or funds rather than by owning a unit.

body.title: Calculate: Rent on a Mall Store
body.prompt: A fashion brand in a Hyderabad mall has a lease with a minimum guarantee of ₹2,00,000 a month or 10% of sales, whichever is higher. This month the store sold ₹25,00,000. How much rent does the owner receive?
body.explanation: 10% of ₹25,00,000 = ₹2,50,000, which is higher than the ₹2,00,000 minimum guarantee, so rent is ₹2,50,000. If sales had been ₹15,00,000, the revenue share would be ₹1,50,000 and the owner would receive the ₹2,00,000 minimum.

body.title: Quick Check: Efficiency
body.question: Building A quotes ₹100 per sq ft of chargeable area with 80% efficiency. Building B quotes ₹90 per sq ft with 68% efficiency. Which is cheaper per usable sq ft?
options: Building B, because its quoted rent is lower
Building A, at ₹125 per usable sq ft versus about ₹132 for Building B
It cannot be calculated without the carpet area in sq ft
body.explanation: Building A: ₹100 ÷ 0.80 = ₹125. Building B: ₹90 ÷ 0.68 = about ₹132.4. The lower quote hides worse efficiency, so Building A gives more usable space per rupee.

body.title: Scenario: Three Commercial Pitches
body.scenario: Farhan, a Mumbai business owner, has ₹2.5 crore to invest. He receives three pitches. (1) A 1,200 sq ft chargeable strata office in a 15-year-old Andheri East building, leased at ₹1.5 lakh a month. (2) A 400 sq ft ground-floor shop on a busy Thane high street, leased to a pharmacy chain at ₹1.4 lakh a month. (3) A unit in a new strata-sold mall on the city outskirts, where the developer promises an "assured return" of 12% a year, ₹2.5 lakh a month, for three years.
body.prompt: Compare the three. Which pitch should worry him most, and why?
body.modelAnswer: The office yields ₹18 lakh ÷ ₹2.5 crore = 7.2%, and the shop ₹16.8 lakh ÷ ₹2.5 crore = 6.72%. Both are in a normal range. The office needs checks on building vacancy, upkeep, efficiency and tenant strength. The shop yields slightly less but has a strong tenant and a location driven by footfall that is usually easier to re-let and sell. The mall pitch should worry him most. A 12% "assured return" is far above market commercial yields, so it is almost certainly built into an inflated price, and it lasts only three years. After that, rent depends on a new strata-sold mall attracting footfall with no single owner managing it. If market rent then turns out to be ₹80,000 a month, and buyers value it at an 8% cap rate, the unit is worth ₹9.6 lakh ÷ 0.08 = ₹1.2 crore. He would have received ₹90 lakh in assured payments but lost ₹1.3 crore of capital, and that assumes the developer keeps paying for the full three years at all.

body.title: Before Buying Any Commercial Unit
steps: Confirm occupancy certificate, fire NOC and commercial land use approvals
Find out who owns the rest of the building: a single owner or many strata owners
Check current vacancy in the building and the immediate neighbourhood
Calculate efficiency and compare rent per usable sq ft with competing buildings
Review maintenance charges and who manages common areas
Check power load, parking, lifts and floor plate size against likely tenant needs
For shops, stand outside at different times of day and watch footfall and visibility
Treat any "assured return" offer as a red flag and ask what the price would be without it

cards.definition: Individual units in one building sold to different owners, fragmenting control of the building.
The area on which office rent is charged, including a share of common spaces.
Carpet area divided by chargeable area; how much of the paid-for space is usable.
A mall lease where rent is the higher of a fixed minimum or a percentage of store sales.
A property constructed to a specific tenant's requirements in exchange for a long lease.
A developer's promise of fixed payments for a set period, often priced into an inflated purchase price.

points: In commercial property, who controls the rest of the building matters as much as the unit you buy.
Grade A offices are mostly institutionally owned and accessed through REITs; individuals usually buy strata offices with smaller tenants.
Office rent is quoted on chargeable area, so always convert it to rent per usable sq ft using efficiency.
High-street shop value rests on footfall, frontage and visibility, which can shift with new infrastructure.
Strata-sold malls often fail because no one controls tenant mix; successful malls stay with a single professional owner.
Warehouses are land-heavy, long-lease assets dominated by institutional developers, with approval risks in older unorganised stock.

body.text: Rents, efficiency ranges, yields and valuations in this lesson are illustrative and vary by city, building and lease. Company names are used as examples only. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy any property or security.
